clinicalPearls: X-linked protoporphyria is a cutaneous porphyria caused by gain-of-function variants in ALAS2 (erythroid-specific delta-aminolaevulinic acid synthase), typically small deletions in the final exon that remove the enzyme's autoregulatory carboxy-terminus and increase its activity.

It is clinically indistinguishable from erythropoietic protoporphyria: acute, painful, non-blistering photosensitivity with burning, stinging and swelling of sun-exposed skin, often beginning in early childhood.

Increased ALAS2 activity drives excess protoporphyrin production in erythroid cells, so both metal-free protoporphyrin and zinc-protoporphyrin accumulate — unlike classic EPP where the zinc-chelated fraction is comparatively low.
Diagnosis rests on a raised erythrocyte total protoporphyrin with a substantially higher proportion of zinc-protoporphyrin than in FECH-related EPP, confirmed by ALAS2 molecular testing.

Because it is X-linked, hemizygous males are usually affected, while heterozygous females show variable severity depending on lyonisation; this differs from the autosomal recessive/dominant inheritance of erythropoietic protoporphyria.
Hepatobiliary complications from protoporphyrin deposition — cholelithiasis and potentially severe protoporphyric liver disease — occur as in EPP and warrant periodic liver monitoring.
Excess protoporphyrin is excreted in bile and faeces, not urine, so urinary porphyrins and porphyrin precursors are characteristically normal and do not exclude the diagnosis.

Management centres on strict visible-light photoprotection, opaque physical sunblocks and clothing, correction of any coexisting iron deficiency, and consideration of afamelanotide or other photoprotective strategies in specialist centres.
reference.pathophysiology: X-linked protoporphyria is caused by gain-of-function variants in ALAS2 on the X chromosome, which encodes the erythroid-specific isoform of delta-aminolaevulinic acid synthase, the first and rate-limiting enzyme of the haem biosynthetic pathway in developing red cells. The commonest variants are small frameshift deletions in the terminal exon that truncate the enzyme's carboxy-terminal regulatory domain; loss of this autoinhibitory tail markedly increases catalytic activity and the flux of delta-aminolaevulinic acid entering the pathway. The downstream enzymes, particularly ferrochelatase, become rate-limiting, so metal-free protoporphyrin IX accumulates in erythrocytes and, because ferrochelatase activity is normal rather than deficient, a substantial fraction is also chelated with zinc to form zinc-protoporphyrin — the biochemical signature that separates this disorder from ferrochelatase-deficient erythropoietic protoporphyria. Lipophilic protoporphyrin released from red cells circulates in plasma and, on absorbing visible light in the Soret band around the violet region, generates reactive oxygen species that damage vascular endothelium and dermal tissue, producing the intense burning photosensitivity. Protoporphyrin is cleared hepatically into bile, where high concentrations can be cholestatic and crystallise, driving gallstones and, in a minority, progressive protoporphyric hepatopathy that may culminate in liver failure. Availability of iron modulates the phenotype, since iron limitation further favours accumulation of metal-free protoporphyrin.
additionalDifferentials: Erythropoietic protoporphyria due to ferrochelatase (FECH) deficiency
Polymorphic light eruption and solar urticaria
Congenital erythropoietic porphyria and porphyria cutanea tarda (blistering cutaneous porphyrias)
Contact or atopic dermatitis of sun-exposed skin
additionalInvestigations: Erythrocyte total protoporphyrin with fractionation into metal-free and zinc-protoporphyrin
Plasma porphyrin fluorescence scan showing an emission peak around the protoporphyrin wavelength
ALAS2 molecular genetic testing, including terminal-exon deletion analysis
Iron studies and ferritin to identify contributory iron deficiency
Liver function tests and hepatic imaging for protoporphyric liver disease and gallstones
Faecal porphyrins (raised) with confirmation that urinary porphyrins are normal
FECH gene analysis to distinguish from erythropoietic protoporphyria when needed
redFlags: Rising bilirubin or transaminases suggesting protoporphyric liver injury
Rapidly progressive cholestasis or signs of acute hepatic decompensation
Severe unremitting phototoxic pain with skin breakdown
Right upper quadrant pain indicating symptomatic gallstones
New anaemia or worsening iron status altering protoporphyrin balance
reference.prognosis: Most patients have a lifelong but non-progressive cutaneous course dominated by disabling photosensitivity and marked lifestyle restriction, with normal life expectancy when the liver is unaffected. A minority develop serious protoporphyric hepatopathy that can progress to liver failure and require transplantation, making periodic hepatic surveillance essential.
pitfalls: Excluding porphyria on the basis of normal urinary porphyrins, which are expected to be normal in this erythropoietic protoporphyria variant
Assuming ferrochelatase deficiency and stopping the workup without measuring the zinc-protoporphyrin fraction or testing ALAS2
Overlooking the diagnosis in an affected female by assuming a purely recessive X-linked pattern
Neglecting liver monitoring and missing early protoporphyric hepatopathy
Aggressively correcting iron without recognising its influence on protoporphyrin accumulation and photosensitivity

management: Strict photoprotection with sun avoidance, tightly woven protective clothing and opaque reflectant sunblocks as the mainstay
The alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone analogue afamelanotide to increase dermal melanin and improve light tolerance
Oral beta-carotene and correction of the vitamin D deficiency arising from sun avoidance
Identification and correction of contributory iron deficiency
Periodic liver function testing and hepatic imaging to detect protoporphyric liver disease and gallstones
Prompt hepatology referral for progressive protoporphyric hepatopathy, which may require intensive treatment or liver transplantation
Genetic counselling with ALAS2 testing and assessment of variably affected female carriers
